Rent or buy? Compare the housing budget, invested savings and exit costs

Explore four charts that give renting and buying the same starting capital and monthly budget, then track debt, carrying costs and invested differences.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore renting and buying with a common budget

Interactive planning lab

Starting capital in either case$132,000
Owner ending wealth$360,031.78
Renter ending portfolio$287,564.12

Hypothetical comparable housing over the selected years. Mortgage: 25-year amortization, nominal quoted rate compounded semi-annually, constant throughout. Renter invests the owner’s down payment plus purchase costs. Each month both households allocate the higher housing cash outflow; the cheaper option invests the difference at month-end. Investment returns are effective annual rates before tax and fees. Owner costs scale with current home value; rent increases annually. Owner wealth assumes sale at every displayed endpoint. No default insurance, tax benefits, capital-gains tax, moving costs or rent-law constraints are modeled.

The central idea

The comparison depends on the full cash flows and the holding period. Include the down payment’s alternative use, ownership costs and the costs of leaving.

01

Give both households the same starting resources

A useful comparison begins with homes that provide comparable housing services and households that start with the same money. A larger property with a different location or quality changes the living arrangement as well as the financing decision.

The buyer uses starting capital for the down payment and purchase costs. The renter invests that same capital. In the default example, a CAD 600,000 home, 20% down payment and 2% purchase costs require CAD 132,000. The mortgage begins at CAD 480,000; the renter’s investment portfolio begins at CAD 132,000.

The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s homebuying guide emphasizes costs beyond the mortgage and lists examples of closing expenses. The percentages in these charts are hypothetical placeholders. They are not quotations for transfer tax, legal fees, commissions or a particular transaction.

02

Invest the cost advantage in either direction

Every month, the tool calculates each household’s housing cash outflow. It gives both households a common budget equal to the higher amount. Whichever option is cheaper invests the difference at month-end. This can be the renter or the owner, and the direction can change as rent and owner costs evolve.

The owner pays mortgage principal and interest plus combined carrying costs. The carrying-cost assumption is a yearly percentage of the current modeled home value, allocated monthly. It can stand for a budget allowance for property tax, insurance, maintenance and similar expenses, but those actual bills need their own estimates.

The renter pays the selected rent, increasing once a year at the assumed rate. The FCAC renting guide notes that additional rental expenses depend on the arrangement. Shared utilities and lifestyle costs are omitted here as equal in both cases. Add a difference to the budget before applying the comparison to unlike living arrangements.

03

Distinguish the cash required from the cost consumed

The first-year bars compare average monthly housing outflows before investing any cost difference. Mortgage principal is included because it must be paid, but it also reduces debt. Therefore, the outflow bars are not a pure economic-expense comparison between rent and interest.

The mortgage uses a 25-year amortization and the same explicit semi-annual quoted-rate convention as the renewal guide. Its rate remains unchanged for the entire selected comparison. That simplifies the calculation but leaves renewal uncertainty out. Actual future payments may differ.

Both portfolios earn the same effective annual investment return, converted to a monthly rate. Home value also changes smoothly each month at the selected annual assumption. Repairs can be uneven, investments fluctuate and neither growth rate is assured. A smooth path is a calculation convention, not a forecast of the experience of either household.

04

Compare the resources available after an exit

The owner’s line equals home value less assumed sale costs and outstanding mortgage debt, plus any investment portfolio accumulated from a monthly cost advantage. The renter’s line is the investment portfolio. Every point on the owner’s line assumes a sale at that date, including the starting point.

That sale convention means the buyer starts below the renter after transaction costs. Purchase costs have been consumed, and the chart also allows for a hypothetical immediate sale cost. Longer holding periods give other cash flows and value changes more time to matter; they do not guarantee that either option wins.

With the default assumptions, modeled year-ten resources are CAD 360,031.78 for the owner and CAD 287,564.12 for the renter. The waterfall reconciles the home value, sale costs, debt and both portfolios to show the difference. The endpoint measures relative modeled wealth, not the home’s investment profit or an annual return.

05

Test assumptions that could reverse the comparison

The matrix reruns the monthly comparison for different home-value changes and investment returns. Each signed cell is owner ending wealth minus renter ending wealth. It also recalculates the carrying costs tied to modeled home value. A positive result favors the owner within the model; a negative result favors the renter.

Test a shorter stay, higher carrying costs, a weaker home-value path and different rent growth. Consider whether the assumed investments and regular saving would actually be maintained. A renter who spends the cost difference or an owner who faces an unbudgeted major repair follows a different path.

The model excludes taxes and housing benefits, default insurance, moving expenses, detailed condominium assessments, rent-law constraints and the costs of mortgage changes. Its minimum down-payment input of 20% avoids modeling insured-mortgage premiums but does not establish eligibility or approval. Flexibility, location, stability and the household’s other goals also deserve weight. Use actual comparable-home costs and current contract terms before making the commitment.
